utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. And on behalf of the Chamber, I wish you all the best for the coming year, and I hope that you had some time to relax. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue with the cross-examination of Witness DFS-014. There are a few procedural matters I would like to address. The first is about the witness order in the week, this week, beginning the 9th of January, 2012. On the last day of court before the winter recess, the Simatovic Defence asked the Chamber to accommodate Witness DFS-014 by recommencing his testimony in the week starting on the 16th of January, 2012, because of Orthodox Christmas and New Year, which the witness observes. The Chamber was therefore requested not to sit in the week of the 9th of January. The Chamber, through an informal communication, informed the parties on the 21st of December, 2011, of its decision that Witness DFS-014 should reappear on the 10th of January. Due to its concerns about significant loss of court time, the Chamber requested that the Defence bring a second witness to testify in that week, once Witness DFS-014 had completed his testimony. The Chamber also requested the Victims and Witness Section to organise the Witness DFS-014's transport so as to least interfere with his Orthodox Christmas celebrations. As for the appearance of a second witness during that week, there was further informal communication about the possibility of the Stanisic Defence Witness Brown being called. However, after both the Prosecution and the Stanisic Defence raised concerns about this option, the Chamber decided not to pursue the matter further. With both the Stanisic and the Simatovic Defence having pursued other possible options to no avail, a second witness will not appear this week. I'd like now move to the second item, which is the witness scheduling for the upcoming weeks. In an informal communication, the Chamber also requested that the Simatovic and Stanisic Defence provide information today about the scheduling of witnesses for the upcoming weeks. And, therefore, I'd like to hear from the parties. The last update we received is the 6th of January, which says that Witness DFS-014 would testify this week. And I'd like to know how much time the Stanisic Defence would need for the cross-examination of DFS-014.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and Happy New Year to Your Honours. One and a half hours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One and a half hours. Prosecution, any indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not having heard the Stanisic cross-examination, I anticipate two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two hours. Then, for next week Witness DFS-013 and Witness DFS-001 have been scheduled; three hours for examination-in-chief for both the witnesses. Is that still as matters stand, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any indication about cross-examination of Witness DFS-013?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I consider that and inform Your Honours at the break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, Your Honour, but I would anticipate approximately the same time as Mr. Petrovic takes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another three hours. Witness DFS-001, matters still -- still three hours, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. Our final proofing is still pending with the witness, so it is possible that the time may be a bit shorter or a bit longer. But that would be approximately the time that we have envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the Stanisic Defence, same request?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, the same comment, Your Honour. I would anticipate the same amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, for the week after that, Witness DFS-009, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have a list on me, but the time will not change. The witness has confirmed his arrival. I would kindly ask you to leave the room to the Defence to either increase or decrease the time closer to the day of the witness's testimony and after our final proofing exercise is completing -- completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, for that week, four hours is reserved by the Simatovic Defence for Witness DFS-009. And on my list I see that for Witness DFS-017 the same time has been claimed, four hours as well. We'll leave it for the time being. Mr. Petrovic, Witness DFS-014, we had the experience that you've covered quite some matters which were not in dispute. Would you, in preparing for your next witnesses, keep that in mind very much. The Chamber is not here to hear testimony about matters which are not in dispute between the parties. And it was not only once, but it happened more than once that I had to remind you of that during the examination-in-chief of Witness DFS-014. I leave it to that for the time being. Could we receive soon, Mr. Petrovic, the follow-up, because we have now covered the period up to and including 26th of January, and that the Chamber is informed as soon as possible about the beginning of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Petrovic, the Prosecution has filed an urgent Prosecution motion to compel Simatovic Defence to provide information about source materials used by its MUP expert, and motion for extension of time to file a 94 bis response. In an informal communication, the Chamber has requested you to submit your position not later than by today. Do you intend to make these submissions orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is the way I understood your instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed and tell the Chamber what the position of the Simatovic Defence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, I would like to say that our Defence is doing its utmost to comply with the parts of the requests of our learned friends from the Prosecution. Those requests are more or less founded, and we're trying to comply with them. However, we should bear in mind the fact that we're talking about an expert who has his team and who is trying to deliver on what we have asked him to do. However, we cannot influence his organisation of time and his priorities, although we have asked him to do it in the shortest possible time and to do it fully and completely. As far as Mr. Groome's request for an additional deadline, we do not oppose to that. Our experts will be called at the end of the Defence case. When we comply with our obligation, we believe that our learned friends from the Prosecution will have ample time to prepare adequately for the cross-examination. In addition to that, we would kindly ask our learned friends from the OTP to identify some parts of the report, based on the report, which are not in dispute, some parts that may be accepted, or those parts that don't have to be corroborated by other evidence. This would probably reduce the number of documents that would accompany the report, and this would also speed up the testimony of the witness and the acceptance and the admittance of his report. Most of the sources which are still missing at this moment are the sources that are relative to the introductory part of the expert report and schedule number 1 that accompanies the report. I'm sure that you have seen that schedule number 1 is a historical overview of events. Those parts of the report which, according to our view, are the most important and which are probably in dispute and refer to the majority of the evidence, those parts of the report have already been filed. The least number of the sources that are still missing belong to the parts which speak about the organisation and the functioning of the state security of Serbia between 1991 and 1995 and those that are relative to Franko Simatovic himself. The expert report is -- has 476 footnotes. At this moment, we are missing 45 documents. All the other documents have already been admitted as P or D documents, or are documents on the 65 ter lists either of the Prosecution or the Stanisic Defence or on our 65 ter list. We have entered P, D, and 65 ter documents in the report to help all the parties. We have not provided our colleagues from the Prosecution with that version because we wanted to finalize the procedure to enter all the evidence and, thus, to avoid having several versions of the expert report at the same time. However, if the Trial Chamber and our learned friends from the OTP consider that that would be of some help to them, we can submit a -- the version which is still not complete and which might facilitate their preparation. However, having said that, several versions may bring confusion into the whole matter. But if this is the position of the Trial Chamber and the OTP, we can provide the parties with the incomplete version and by -- having said that, I mean that not all the documents have been entered. 45 documents are missing. All of them, except for six that we are still awaiting, will be uploaded before the end of day tomorrow as 2D documents, and those 2D markings will also be entered into the expert report text. The 46 documents in question, or, rather, the 39 documents in question will be submitted for translation and we will ask for urgency in dealing with these documents for the benefit of the OTP. I would like to say that the documents that are missing are legal texts which are not in dispute, which are publicly available, but I'm not saying this to diminish our responsibility or anything like that. I'm just saying that as the text itself is concerned, they are not in dispute. Their interpretation, however, may be in dispute. The interpretation of legal text and other legal documents is exactly the subject of our expert's testimony. As for the attachments to the expert report, which is schedule 2, there are seven graphs. They have been uploaded. They have been translated. They can be found in the system. And they're readily available to the parties as we speak. In conclusion, I would like to say we know what our responsibility is. We are doing or utmost to comply with it. And we believe that we will be able to comply all of the requests of our colleagues from the OTP in the shortest possible time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understood the Prosecution well, Mr. Petrovic, they said, Whether we can agree with the conclusions of the report, yes or no, depends on the material underlying the report. Now, you're saying if the Prosecution would already agree to some parts of the report, that there would be less need to be provided with the underlying documentation, which is putting the arguments upside down. That's one observation. The second one I'd like to make is, you say 45 or 39 documents are still missing, but this is all publically available and these are all legal texts. I must say that I'm a bit surprised. That if it's publically available and these are legal texts, why are they not, then, provided without any delay to the Prosecution? Is it about translations? Because I didn't hear you say anything about translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I said that they were publicly available, I wanted to say that it is not our obligation to provide them. It is our obligation -- what I was saying was that they're not in dispute. What may be in dispute is their interpretation. The parts of the expert report that are based on those texts may be in dispute from the point of view of their interpretation but not from the point of view of the source of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say only 45 are missing or 39 are still missing. Does the Prosecution know by now which are the missing ones and which are available? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to check with what precision we know what the documents are actually missing. I know that a substantial number of documents are missing, and it's a very sizeable report so it really has hampered our ability to evaluate the report. And I would note that the Chamber is correct. Our concern not is -- is not insomuch our ability to cross-examine or prepare for cross-examination, but is simply to fulfil our obligations under 94 bis and to let the Chamber know whether we're going to contest the report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it assist you if Mr. Petrovic would provide with you a copy of the report in which D, P, and 65 ter numbers are included?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He has mentioned that many of them are. To the extent that he can point that out to us, then that would obviate the need for him to re-serve them on us. We can find them ourselves in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, this sounds like an invitation. And Mr. Groome apparently is less concerned about being confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the one other thing that I would point out is that we would ask that the 30 days that we are afforded under the Rules commence when Mr. Petrovic certifies to the Chamber that he has served all these documents. We will, of course, endeavour to evaluate the report in a shorter period and give our response to it. I would also acknowledge and thank Mr. Petrovic for his commitment to provide drafts of the report. That may also assist us in our evaluation of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, having heard the parties, and the Stanisic Defence may have -- may take no position in this? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Exactly so, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would be inclined to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decides that we leave it in the hands of the parties for a while and therefore will not decide on the motion yet, but the Chamber would appreciate if it would be informed as soon as possible if the developments as more or less sketched by Mr. Petrovic would not materialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, so my silence is not misinterpreted: Mr. Petrovic several times indicated that the documents were not in dispute; until we've had a chance to see them and evaluate them, we aren't able to say whether or not they are in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. But you can live with the situation where the Chamber postpones the decision on your motion in view of the answer given by Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Chamber is not bound to -- or the Prosecution is not bound to file a response in the time specified by Rule 94 bis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that request, of course, would then be -- a decision on that -- postponing a decision on that would not mean that you are under an obligation to file within 30 days your position. That would be -- if it ever comes to a final decision on the motion, if the matter is not settled by the parties meanwhile, then you'll be excused for not having filed within 30 days the -- response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the response. Then the next brief item is: On the 12th of December, 2011, Serbia has requested protective measures for a number of documents. Now, one of these documents has already been admitted into evidence as a public exhibit, and accordingly, in order not to frustrate a possible later decision granting protective measures, P992 is provisionally put under seal. Then, finally, I put on the record that the Chamber - and I take it the parties are aware of it - has received notice that by the -- by CMSS, that the guarantees by the Republic of Serbia necessary to give effect to the Chamber's decision on the provisional release for Mr. Simatovic, that those guarantees have not been received, and that for that reason Mr. Simatovic has not left the Detention Unit and could not spend time in Belgrade but had to stay in The Hague. The Chamber is, of course, totally unaware of the reasons for it, but that's the situation. It was one of the conditions under which the Chamber granted provisional release for Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honour: We are, at the moment, keeping things under advisement, in the sense that we didn't receive any response from the Serbian government. And we are looking into that and considering filing a motion. Of course, if -- we don't submit that the Serbian government has to issue guarantees, but arguably, the Serbian government has to respond, so we're looking into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then wait what further steps you'll initiate. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to say that when we received your decision about the temporary release of Mr. Simatovic, we addressed the Government of the Republic of Serbia and its institutions in writing, and we asked for formal reasons why they are denying what we believe is their legal obligation and that is to provide guarantees. Unfortunately, until this very day we have not received any answer. We have not been given any reason why the legal obligation has not been complied with and why Mr. Simatovic has not been given the guarantees that, in our view, he is perfectly entitled to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, since you mentioned twice, or you used the phrase "legal obligations," the Chamber, of course, and the law of the Tribunal, finds no legal obligations. The Chamber can grant provisional release under certain conditions, and the conditions are not phrased in such a way in the law of the Tribunal that it is a legal obligation, but that it is within the discretion of the state concerned whether or not to grant those guarantees. Again, whether there's any obligation under domestic law is a different matter. But I would like to put clearly on the record that, whether any legal obligations for Serbia do exist, that by not further commenting on it, the Chamber does not accept that under the law of the Tribunal such obligations do exist. I leave it open. If there will be ever any further issue about it, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Chamber, if -- if required, will determine the matter, but, until now, the Chamber was not required to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for your comment. Naturally, I didn't think that it was a matter of an obligation based on the Rules of the Tribunal. It's based on the internal laws of the Republic of Serbia. That's what I had in mind. According to the constitution and the laws of Serbia, the Republic of Serbia had the obligation to issue such guarantees. But naturally, on this occasion, we will address the Chamber about the issue at an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber refrains from any comments at this moment on this matter. Anything else to be raised? If not, then could I ask Witness DFS-014 to be escorted into the courtroom. Are all the protective measures in place, Madam Registrar? That is, face distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym? Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know, while the witness is being brought in, whether I can update you in relation to our three outstanding witnesses. I should have jumped up quicker. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the witness will enter the courtroom in a second. And if there -- it's about three witnesses, then we'll find, later today or at least this week, we'll find time to hear your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DFS-014.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you started your testimony prior to the recess, not very long ago, I think that it would be sufficient at this moment to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given. That is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. First of all, I would like to express the appreciation of the Chamber, that finally you are willing to come back so soon after Orthodox Christmas. We tried to do our utmost best to see whether your travelling would interfere minimally in celebrating the Orthodox Christmas. Nevertheless, I would like to express the appreciation of the Chamber. Witness DFS-014, may I remind you that during the examination-in-chief and it happened a couple of times that through your answers that there was a, although slight, risk of at least giving a clue to identifying yourself, and I would like to emphasise again that if there's anything in your answers which is creating a risk of undermining your pseudonym, that you should ask for private session. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. You may proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't think there's anything that you've said so far which we disagree with. I just want to seek some clarification on a number of issues. First issue is this: That you spoke about the calling up or the mobilising of the reserve police force at the Knin Police Station in 1990 around the time of the erection of the roadblocks; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's, Your Honours, page 15772.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you spoke about the reserve force being paid by the companies where they had been permanently -- or where they were permanently employed; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such were the rules throughout Yugoslavia that concerned the reserve forces. When there are reserve forces, they would be mobilized, and they would be paid by the companies that employed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And throughout 1990, are you able to recall - and I'm talking about a time when the roadblocks were being formed and Knin Police Station had effectively become Serbian populated - can you recall the ratio between the reserve police and the permanently employed police at the Knin Police Station through 1990?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't fully understand you. What do you mean by "ratio" or relationship? Are you talking about employment? What do you have in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, let me clarify that. Numbers. I'm looking at numbers. How many police officers were at the Knin Police Station when you were present, and how many were reserve and how many were fully employed?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, as far as I can remember, there were almost 70 authorised officials, not including civilians and women who had no authority, and there was perhaps between 40 and 50 individuals who were part of the reserve force. They had been called on the 17th of August, around that time, 1990, and this force wasn't disbanded. They remained on active duty throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there a point in time when the reserve force increased from what it had been prior to these events revolving around the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number of reserve forces was increased as well as active police officers. The number of active members was also increased after the SUP in Krajina was established on the 5th of January, 1991. The active police force was also increased in September 1990, throughout that period of time, which is when many inspectors and police officers from other stations in Croatia expressed certain wishes and asked to be transferred to the police station in Knin. And this was authorised. There was a particular event in September 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's just leave it there for now. So is this a fair summary: Up until November 1990 the reserve police in Knin were paid by their companies and the authorised police were paid by the Croatian MUP directly from Zagreb? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, in December of 1990 the situation changed because the salaries stopped coming from Zagreb. Now, just dealing with the reserve police post-November 1990, did they, the ones in Knin, continue to receive their salaries from the companies in the Krajina, the companies which had previously been paying their salaries?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stopped performing the duties I have already mentioned. I wasn't really concerned about keeping track of things, but I know that since money, funds were being collected for active police officers in the station, for us, the active police officers, the reservists were still on the salary rolls, payrolls of the companies they worked for. These companies continued to work, and they paid their employees as well as the reserve members of the police force of the Knin station.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the authorised active police officers, you've spoken about voluntary donations. Do you agree with this: that there was, post-November 1990 and through 1991, a significant amount of humanitarian aid, including food and money, coming into Knin which was used, in part, to finance the police?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that during that period of time we received various kinds of foodstuff, flour, for example, and other provisions. And this was sort of compensation instead of the salary that we didn't receive at the time. We received such things from humanitarian sources. I remember convoys coming from Semberija and Bijeljina. It was winter at the time. It was cold. So there were humanitarian convoys that came from the Banja Luka region, and a reception was organised on that occasion. They would bring in flour, cabbage, meat, and so on and so forth. And this was distributed to the population. And we also received part of that humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So was there a period of time post-November 1990 that the police did not receive a salary in terms of money but received instead only food and other such items to allow them to continue working?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that that was a two- or three-month period during which we didn't receive any salaries, but we received assistance. The first salaries we received were, I think, represented about 6.000 or 6 million and that was a lot lower than the average for employees of certain companies in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was that money coming from voluntary donations from local companies and also from the foreign diaspora?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, Radio Knin was increasingly active, and there was a lot of information disseminated especially in the evening hours. Information according to which a certain village had gathered a certain sum of money for the SUP in Krajina, and this was to include the Knin Police and Benkovac and Obrovac and perhaps funds were also distributed in Lika later on. But they said that villages or companies had amassed a certain amount of money. This would be brought to the Knin station and handed over to us as our salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So is this the way it worked then, that the villages and the towns which were populated by Serbians would collect donations themselves from within their locality and elsewhere, and, at a certain point, it would be brought to the Knin headquarters where it would then be distributed to a number of entities and individuals, including the police?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've summarized that quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, would you please try -- the witness, in-chief, said that he -- as far as he knew, they got their salaries from donations. Now the witness says about what information was distributed, et cetera. Could we try to find out exactly the concrete knowledge of what actually was collected by the population and what the basis of his knowledge is. Because, at this moment, it's all what he understood to be the case rather than what details he knows about what really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I think you've heard what His Honour, the Judge, just said. Let's try to be as concrete as possible in terms of your knowledge, what you knew, and how you knew it. Perhaps, for a moment, let's go into private session, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now I want to move to another subject, which is the subject of the JNA. And you've told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At, Your Honours, page 15801.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- that at the beginning of September the JNA moved from playing a buffer role to launching an offensive. Did you understand your previous testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood my testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How do you know this? How did you come by this information?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know because at the beginning of September the JNA withdrew from the positions that I myself occupied because there was a threat that their barracks in Sibenik and Zadar would be occupied. And especially the barracks in Sibenik. That's why they organised convoys, and they decided to launch an offensive in the direction of Sibenik to lift the blockade from the barracks. They had a lot of equipment, for example, tanks and cannons and many other things like that, but they did not have enough infantry, which is necessary to support tank operations. That's when they mobilized people, to replenish their units. And people were mobilized from TO units. They were called up to join the units of the JNA and they were placed under the JNA command. After that, they never ever returned under the command of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you -- I want to have you read a part of a diary, the Mladic diary, and see if you can cast any light on some of the information in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please, could we have 65 ter 5596 on the screen. And I'm looking for page 37 of the English and 37 of the typed B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you may not be familiar with these books. I don't know if you've heard of them before, but these are accepted to be -- accepted by the Prosecution and the Defence to be written by Mladic. And I want to ask you if you can comment on any of the entries, or some of the entries. This is an entry of the 31st of August, 1991. And if we -- we don't have the B/C/S yet. Of the typed B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are several documents there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps, while that's coming up, I'll read part of it to you and see if we can speed things up in that way? The entry ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've just been remind of the time. I don't know if that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a convenient moment. It's 75 minutes after we started. We'll take a break. And we resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we -- I think we have the right page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's an entry relating to Saturday, the 31st of August, 1991. And Mladic appears to be having talks with the SAOK, Mandinic. And it's noted towards the bottom of the page under number five that "the JNA units should disinfect the terrain and that the commanders of the units which laid the minefields provide charts of the minefields to the JNA in order for them to be cleared." Were you aware or did you learn about the role of the JNA in this regard at this time?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, JNA units were deployed as buffers. I remember the negotiations in question. They were in the place where I am from. I was in the vicinity. I did not participate in the negotiations, but I was not far away. When it comes to bullet point 5, where it says that the minefields should be cleared, this refers to a situation whereby a local started walking or taking a shortcut towards the place where the negotiations were taking place, and he hit a mine that had probably been placed by the Croatian police. I believe that bullet point 5 refers to that situation because it was then assumed that there were many such mines. Those mines were supposed to removed. And I believe that bullet point 5 reflects that particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You referred to "negotiations." Who are the negotiations between; and what was the object of the negotiations as you understood them to be?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see here, the negotiations involved representatives of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina represented by Neso Mandinic and the representatives of the Croatian MUP represented by Mr. Juras.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. -- let me -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Than was all with the mediation of the JNA. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. Were you aware at the time, then, that the JNA was acting as the mediator between these two opposing sides? Not just from looking at what we have on the screen, but were you aware at that time?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could assume that. I knew it, actually. In that area, immediately before that, perhaps a month before, there was an incident which involved the local population and the representatives of the Croatian police. That incident resulted in some people wounded, and JNA units arrived thereafter in order to curb the situation, and they placed themselves as a buffer between us and the Croatian forces. At that time, Mr. Mladic arrived. He was colonel at the time. I remember his visit. And when he arrived, he would go to the Croatian side and he would warn them through the bull horn not shoot, that there would be negotiations, that he had come to visit the line, and that he was the one who had been tasked with stopping the conflict in the area. That's what he was telling them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That was a month before this entry. Were you aware of Mladic's position at the time of this entry? Had he expressed similar views? Had he behaved in similar ways, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at that time Colonel Mladic was also the Chief of Staff of the 9th Corps of the JNA. He played a neutral role. He tried to separate the warring parties. And in that sense, two tanks, two transporters, and some JNA infantry were deployed between our positions and Croatian positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on in the diary to page 41 at the bottom, which is four pages on. And we'll see there what was apparently, according to Mladic, agreed during these negotiations. The following was adopted in ten points. One - and I'm looking at the bottom of the page - the withdrawal of all Martic's formations from the Sibenik municipality, unconditional - going over the page - adherence to the cease-fire from Drnis to the village of Pristeg. Ensure simul-- number two: Ensure simultaneous return of Serbs and Croats to their villages. And if we -- rather than going through each and every one, if we could then turn to number 6, which is a agreement dependant upon the fulfilment of 1 to 5. If the agreed is implemented, JNA units must be pulled out to the barracks and all their activities reduced to regular ones. Were you aware of this agreement being reached; and were you aware that it was agreed that the JNA would be able to return to normal activities if the two sides implemented the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were stories to that effect. The agreements should have been complied with. And there were stories amongst ourselves, amongst those who lived in the area, about the agreement and about its implementation. However, that never took off the ground. That never came to fruition because a conflict broke out immediately, and its intensity only stepped up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But from what you knew - you agree with this - that both sides who were part of this negotiation, looked at this point in time, end of August, to the JNA to help to broker an agreement, bring about a cease-fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. I agree that the JNA should have played the key role. And that would have been in favour of us surrendering our weapons and the Croatian police leaving the area and also surrendering their weapons. The Croatian police should never have returned to the area, but that came to nothing. Actually, the conflict was intensified a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now let's move forward in this notebook to the 19th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the top of the page is 0668-2799. And it's 65 ter 5596. So we're in the same book. And it's page 72 at the bottom of the page that I'm interested in, relating to the 19th of September. I beg your pardon, sorry, it's -- no. No, that's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, if we just -- if you just read that page. This is, again, Mladic notebook, and he's making notes reflecting things which, it seems, need to be done at this point in time, 19th of September, 1991. And if we go over the page to where Mladic is recording, it seems, his own speech. And Mladic is saying, for example: "Corps commander's working map on the table and a person to be in charge of it. "That the commander be periodically informed on the situation on the front. "During the day we will be using the consultation method, and once a day we will hold collegium meetings." Then over the page, under the reference "war diary": "Each order and request issued by the commander are to be written down. "You will work in your offices. "That a press centre be set up. "That a mobilisation plan be initiated in the operations centre. "That mobilisation progress reports be delivered. "Orders in the corps are issued by the commander and the assistant commander for logistics and, in my absence, by the Chief of Staff." And then over the page, under the title "situation": "Mobilisation is our first task. Work on that tonight. A company may be composed of three platoons, battalions and two companies." Now, I suggest, Mr. Witness, that this is reflective of a sudden move towards an offensive -- offensive actions by the JNA. Did you see anything on the ground to reflect what this diary appears to say concerning mobilisation, concerning getting -- commencing a war diary and so on, on the 19th of September?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I remember the exact date now, whether it was the 19th of September or not, but I did know that mobilisation was being carried out and that it was necessary to do some more intensively, because the battalion command and the command of the JNA units was in the other village, in the vicinity where I was, and occasionally we had meetings. I would go and present the situation. I knew that the unit commander would say that Mladic wasn't happy with the situation with regard to the discipline of the army and so on and so forth. He wasn't happy. Fire would be opened on JNA members. And it was said that the Croatian side couldn't be trusted. At the time it was necessary to remove the blockade of the barracks in Sibenik, and the JNA then took the decision to open up two axes of advance; one in direction of Sibenik, one from Drnis and the other from Vodice. And then these columns were formed. This offence towards Sibenik was a surprise for us. The situation and the combat escalated there, and it was beginning to look like a real war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you say that "Mladic wasn't happy with the situation with regard to the discipline of the army and so on and so forth." How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I went to the command of the unit. The unit was the size of a battalion, and I co-operated with it. And we were in the immediate vicinity of the troops as well. And at the time the troops also counted on our assistance, because they feared a breakthrough on the part of the Croatian units towards themselves and towards ourselves. And at the -- in the army at the time there were also soldiers from Kosovo. There were Muslims from Bosnia. There were Croats as well. And at the time they would desert. They would lay down their arms and cross over to the other side, flee to the other side. I know that the commander said that it was necessary to mobilise local people whom they could trust and who would play the role for which they had been designated, who would carry out orders that were issued to them. Every now and then, several soldiers would desert. Albanians, Muslims, and Croats would desert and they would flee from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was one of the things that Mladic wasn't happy with was it the unity of command? Mladic wanted, at this point in time, the JNA having entered the war, to bring about unity of command of the various military formations in the region?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I think Spiro Nikovic was at the head of the corps. He didn't show much interest for peace in the area. At least he didn't take certain measures. And during that period of time Mladic was more active. The people liked to listen to Mladic. Nikovic didn't even go into the field. And soon after that the corps commander in the area was replaced. Certain offensive operations were carried out by the JNA in the direction of Sibenik and Zadar. And throughout the front line of 100 kilometres or so covered by the Knin Corps there was such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we move on in the book, in the Mladic diary, to page 155, the bottom. At the top is 0668-2799. And it relates to 28th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I just want you to read this bit, the second half of the page, just to get some context. Where Mladic writes: "Invite to a planned meeting someone from the 5th air force command and anti-aircraft defence to be given targets in Zadar." And then over the page. In the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- it's page 156. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we -- once you've read that, we can go over the page.

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we can see over the page at number 5, I'm hoping, where Mladic notes that President Babic has a meeting with presidents of municipalities being scheduled - and for when - regarding mobilisation. And then under that you see a reference to General Spiro, who I think you've just mentioned, getting in touch with Milan Babic, or Milan Babic to get in touch with General Spiro. Do you know if Spiro had been actually in touch with Babic before this, or was this at the time when the real co-ordination began?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about contact between General Spiro and Milan Babic. I know nothing about them having contact. So with regard to this comment, there's nothing I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Let's go over to the page and see number 16, where, as part of this list of things which Mladic seems to be suggesting should happen, we have number 16, where it says -- sorry. Let's -- let's go -- forget about that. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go instead to page 307, the same document, which is 0668-2799. 308 in B/C/S. This is the -- an entry for the 16th of -- 6th of November, 1991. And we see, at this point, there appears to be some, according to Mladic, some kind of unity of command amongst all these groups. Are you able to say, from where you were working and living, approximately when this type of unity of command existed within the Krajina? And when I say "this type," I mean under the command of the JNA, all these forces which we see listed here, being subordinated to, at least -- at least on paper, supposed to be subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the place and time, the place I was at the time, I can say that in my area you could already feel this in September and October. And at the beginning of November, on the 1st of November or the 2nd of November, 1991, only some leaders or commanders stayed behind. They no longer had any troops. All the men from the TO had been transferred to JNA units. As far as co-operation is concerned at the time, well, open co-operation commenced between the SAO Krajina militia and the JNA. That was at the beginning of November 1991. There were such cases prior to that date as well. But during this period of time, this was done openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move to a time when you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps we should go into private, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness DFS-014, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Groome. Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: DFS-014, before I ask a number of questions that I have for you today, I want to clarify some points or some evidence that you provided just before the break. And the first question I would have in that regard: Is the Bogunovic you're speaking about Momcilo Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He's no longer alive, is he?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's deceased. He's no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my information is that he died the 1st of February in 1993, just around the time that you were giving evidence about meetings that you attended in -- with him and others. Does that agree with your information about when he died?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the date that you have which relates to his death is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know how he died?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was killed during a breakthrough. A sniper bullet hit him in the aorta and he bled to death. He -- his escort also died as a result of sniper fire. And there was a problem when it came to extracting the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is this the same -- or do you know if this is the same Momcilo Bogunovic who was the commander of JNA forces when they entered Skabrnja on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the same individual is concerned, the one who was involved in Skabrnja in 1991, and who was also involved in a 1993 event.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, earlier today you said that Bogunovic actually gave orders to Captain Dragan and Arkan. And then, at transcript 50, you said Bogunovic's orders were in writing and they were entered in the book of orders. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you recall a specific operation or a date in which there was an order, a written order by Bogunovic, that gave an express order to Arkan or Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't mention any concrete situations now, but Arkan appeared in the territory of Benkovac around the 24th or 25th of January, 1993. And at the time, I -- I think I have to put things this way. We are in open session, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would prefer to go into private session, then we will move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think out of an abundance of caution we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your testimony earlier today, you spoke about an interaction you had with Captain Dragan and his deputies, and my impression of that was that it was plentiful. You had numerous occasions in which you spoke with Captain Dragan and his deputies. Did I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of meetings. I'm not quite sure what "a lot of" means. This is all relative. But there were a number of meetings between myself and Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how about his deputies. Did you have interaction with his deputies?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew some of them. I would meet some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the names of the deputies who you can recall.

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, there was -- or, rather, there were two brothers, called Bozic. One Bozic was a deputy for a certain period of time. And then there was captain. Captain ... I can't remember his surname now. If I saw his name amongst a number of surnames, I'd remember, because I would meet him at that time. You have to understand that during the war-time period, during this five-year period, I met a lot of people. And there were a lot of events. And I can't remember all of this. But I did know them. I knew the Bozic brothers. One of them was his deputy in charge of the -- the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask to return to private session, could I confirm that 6342 is now available?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: DFS-014, in preparation for your testimony, the Simatovic Defence is required by the Rules of this Court to provide a written summary of what they expect your evidence to be. It is ordinarily drafted after the party speaks with the witness. Your summary, provided to us on the 6th of June, 2011, has an assertion in it, and I would like to clarify whether this assertion is accurate. The summary said: "In light of his position," and then it gave your position, "this witness will be able to disclose his knowledge of the reasons and nature of Franko Simatovic's visits to Knin in the period from the end of May until the end of August 1991." My first question is: Is that accurate? Do you believe you are able to provide that type of information between May and August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, from the end of May until August, I did not come across Franko Simatovic anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to your evidence given here today, did you not give evidence that you left the area in early June and then went on and engaged in a business enterprise that had really nothing to do with your prior employment?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your direct evidence on the 15th of December, you gave some evidence about Arkan. I'd like to read the question and answer and then ask you my own follow-up question. At transcript pages 15812 to -13, you were asked the following question: "When Arkan arrived with his unit, who did he report to upon his arrival in Benkovac?" "A. I don't know exactly. I do know that he, with his unit, was accommodated in a hotel in Benkovac," and then you continue to give more information about the hotel. Do you recall being asked that question and giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At that time, did you make any inquiry into who sent Arkan to the Knin or who he reported to?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never thought that I should make any inquiries about Arkan and how he had come to be there. It was a war-struck area, and most of the issues concerning that war area were issues that were dealt with by the military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you had an obligation to. I'm just simply asking whether you did. And can I ask the same question with respect to Captain Dragan: Once you learned of his presence in the area, did you make any inquiry about who sent him or who he was to report to?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I never asked any questions. I never sought any answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, finally, with respect to Mr. Simatovic: Once you had heard that he was in the area, did he make any additional inquiries to determine who sent him and what exactly his business was there?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never asked that. I never sought to establish any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So any information that you're able to provide this Trial Chamber in this regard is the result of a passive process, that is to say that over the course of your work and your travels you came into possession of different pieces of information which you remembered and you've recounted here in court during your evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. I'm not clear about this line of questioning and about this particular answer -- question. What does this question actually mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think what -- the line of questioning is not something to object to unless good reasons are given for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll rephrase the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would suggest that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic does not understand what I'm asking, so I'm going to ask the question in a different way in the event that perhaps you don't understand either. Whatever information you know about Arkan, about Captain Dragan, about Franko Simatovic wasn't the result of any active investigation or inquiry that you did, it was simply information you picked up along the way in an informal way; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Given my observations, my experience, what I perceived, well, these are things that I experienced. I'm telling you about my experience. I didn't speak about these things at a distance of 100 kilometres. I was an active participant in the events. But I didn't carry out the investigations into when such and such a commander appeared, when such and such a volunteer appeared, who sent certain individuals elsewhere. But what I have spoken about is my personal experience. I experienced the conflict between the Serbs and the Croats in my area, where Mladic was a colonel, where tanks were active as well as the air force. There was an attack on Sibenik and on Zadar in the 1990s and an attack on Benkovac and Obrovac in 1995. There were other experiences. So these are all these experiences that I am referring to. And in the course of that period of time I met those people. I slept in the hotel where Arkan was present. I met this captain, Captain Dragan. These are experiences of mine. These aren't rumours. It's not hearsay. It's -- these are things that I observed myself. These are things I actually experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How confident are you that you have a complete picture of what Arkan was doing there, what Captain Dragan was doing there, what Simatovic was doing there? How confident are you that you have a complete understanding of what was taking place?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a hundred per cent precise information about everything that took place, but I'm sure that I know many things. And I have told you about these things that I have experienced. I know a lot more than the common man in that area at the time knew. And I have related my experiences to you in a precise way. I have provided you with my information. So I would say that 95 per cent of what I have informed you of is information that is precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Given all of what you've told us so far, I would like to explore for a few minutes the likelihood that if the State Security Service was operating in the Knin area, whether it is something you would have become aware of during the time that you spent there. Now, would you agree with me that the State Security Service of Serbia, and any country for that matter, their activities, for the most part, are covert, secret activities? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If they were active, it must have been covert. But when I arrived in the 1990s at the place where I worked in Knin, I was warned by my superior from Zagreb and from the State Security Service of Croatia. I was also told by my leaders in Sibenik and Zagreb that I should be careful about certain things. They said that they'd give me information; I would give them information if I knew they were present in the area at the time. So throughout that period of time when I was down there, even when the events were at a very intense stage, I would certainly have known more things, if things were the way you say they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has heard substantial evidence on internal rules, procedures, and practices of the State Security Service designed to keep information confidential, keep it from the public. Do you have any information that would indicate that the Serbian State Security Service followed a different practice while they were in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no such information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This Chamber has also heard substantial evidence on internal procedures and practices designed to compartmentalise information from other members of the Serbian State Security Service who did not have a need to know that information, only the personnel which were approved to have access to information had that access. Do you have any information that would indicate the Serbian state security followed a different practice in Knin?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if you acknowledge that the Serbian State Security Service, as a general practice, operated secretly and that you did not conduct any active inquiry, do you admit that the information that you have is somewhat limited?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I appeared in Knin, I represented the central authorities of Croatia from Zagreb and I acted and implemented their orders, and this contradicts what you have been saying. Don't you think that if I was carrying out such orders I would have been attacked by that service from Serbia or by some of their associates from the Knin area? Don't you think I would have been under pressure from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ... You testified that you heard from -- most likely from colleagues that there was MUP people, some Frenki in the area in 1991, and asked about any further knowledge, you say, I don't know anything about it. Now, I have some difficulties in fully appreciating your answer. If Mr. Groome asked you would you admit that your information is somewhat limited, now you start explaining to us that your information was not somewhat limited because otherwise you would have ... and then there comes a whole theory. But fact, listening to your testimony, is that you say, "I heard about the presence of MUP, some Frenki. I don't know anything about who sent them, what they were there for," et cetera. And then to say, "No, my knowledge was not in any way limited" is difficult to reconcile, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You formulate your questions differently, and it's easier for me to understand the questions you put to me. That's not the case for the Prosecution. It's true that I heard that in the area of Krajina or in Knin in 1991 I heard about the presence of Frenki from the Serbian MUP. I don't know whether anyone else was present in the area, anyone else from the Serbian State Security Service. I'm also sure that I don't have a 100 per cent correct information or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes. If you do not know anything about it apart from the person being present in the area, then to say that it's -- you do not have the 100 per cent correct information, that seems to be logical. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- jump up. But I would object to the way the Prosecution are proceeding. I mean, perhaps the witness could take his headphones off for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your headphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We're dealing in abstract. If the Serbian DB were there and they've just wondering around in Knin for a couple of days, the witness may have complete knowledge. His testimony may cover the whole activity of the Serbian DB. Alternatively, the Prosecution theory, that the DB had a special unit which was commanding 5.000 soldiers, and so on and so forth, the witness's answer is going to be completely different. Why doesn't the Prosecution put their case so the witness can say, "Yes, I would have known this" or "No, I wouldn't have known that," rather than dancing around the subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent the witness says that he doesn't have full information or that his knowledge may be limited, to draw any conclusions from such testimony takes a careful analysis. And the Chamber will make that analysis. And if it is left all vague, then this may have an impact on the analysis and the conclusions. If that is what you wanted to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put on your earphones again. Yes. Mr. Groome, it is both the question put by Mr. Jordash more or less to you, and my answer may be of some guidance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the record records you as having said just a few moments ago: "It's true that I heard that in the area of the Krajina or in Knin in 1991 I heard about the presence of Frenki from the Serbian MUP." That's at line -- page 82. Is that accurate? Is it -- is the information about Frenki's presence something that you received from members of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that from a member of the MUP in Serbia. I heard it from colleagues from the MUP in the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In fact, in your evidence last December you testified that no one from the Serbian MUP ever came to see you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. No representatives of the Serbian MUP came at the time in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I remind you that we're in open --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we -- first I would like to clarify one matter. And I again would like to -- the witness to take his earphones off. Is my understanding of the English language correct, that the line "I heard about the presence of Frenki from the Serbian MUP" is an ambiguous line which could mean either I heard about the presence of Frenki from someone of the Serbian MUP who told me that, or it could mean I heard about the presence of Frenki who was, in my information, linked to the Serbian MUP? Mr. Groome, I'd like to avoid whatever misunderstandings which may result from ambiguous language. And also because I do not know what the original words of the witness would have been, if he used the one, it could be translated as from a member of the -- Frenki from the Serbian MUP, or if he said the other, it may be translated in the same way, and, therefore, I intervened for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's precisely why I asked the question, because it seemed to be at odds with what the witness had said five, ten minutes ago. So I wanted to give him an opportunity to clarify. He had said earlier today that he heard it from his colleagues. And this was ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you just wanted to take him back to his original answer. At least you wanted to avoid that this new answer could be misunderstood --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could you please put your earphones on again. Yes, the best way of asking would have been: Did you mean this or did you mean that? That's -- Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your evidence, you make repeated statements that you did not hear of activities by Frenki Simatovic, that you did not see him. Is it not correct that you simply were not fully informed about his activities during that period?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's quite possible that he could have been doing all sorts of things that you simply have no knowledge about?

utterances.speaker: DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would like now to explore this issue from the perspective of the Serbian State Security Service and whether at that time they would have considered you to be someone they would feel comfortable sharing secret information with. And this will involve questions about what they knew about you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask that we go into private session to discuss this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps before we do so, I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether starting this line of questioning at three minutes to 7.00 would be wise, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it would be wiser to take it up fresh in the morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, then I would first like to instruct the witness. We'll continue tomorrow, Witness DFS-014, and that will be tomorrow in the morning, at 9.00 in this same courtroom. And I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with anyone about your testimony, whether given either in December or this year, or testimony still to be given. And before we adjourn, I would invite the usher already to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, may I express some concern about what you announced that you would do. Because to ask the witness why others would consider it wiser not to inform the witness about all kind of things he says he was not informed about might be an exercise which may become more argumentative than eliciting knowledge from the witness. I express this concern, leave it to you to think it over until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll just say at this juncture, Your Honour, that my line of questioning will be based on his prior testimony where he gave evidence about how people saw him and how he saw others there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. As long as we keep it factual and as long -- I said I expressed some concerns; of course, I do not know what the questions will be. But you would agree with me that there is a risk, perhaps not with you, but if you only are aware of what you announced you would do, that there is a risk that you end up in guessing about what other people might have thought about what to do and what not to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can assure the Court that I have no intention of doing any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can adjourn. We adjourn for the day. And we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 11th of January of this year, 2012, 9.00 in the morning, same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of January, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
